content: Efforts to address leprosy have focused on targeted areas through active screening and ensuring 100% treatment completion. In the first year of implementation, awareness campaigns followed by active case finding were conducted across eight provinces, leading to the detection of 1,488 new leprosy cases. These cases were provided with multidrug therapy (MDT). This represents a 75% increase in case detection compared to the previous year. Soon, treatment outcomes for patients with paucibacillary (PB) leprosy will be available to assess improvements in case management quality. In 2016, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) planned to expand active screening activities to additional regions as part of a multi-year project. Investigations and screenings were conducted in response to leprosy detection in children, including family and community screenings. Silent communities near endemic areas or those with similar social and infrastructure conditions were also targeted. Leprosy was integrated into the curricula for clinical nurses and medical doctors, including specialized fields like dermatology. Countries with high endemicity or areas with high Grade 2 Disability (G2D) due to weak health systems were identified. Some regions, known as silent zones, had stopped reporting leprosy cases, necessitating verification of zero transmission or identification of gaps in detection and reporting. Each country was tasked with mapping its situation and planning activities accordingly. In Cambodia, the leprosy program, in collaboration with the Novartis Foundation and CIOMAL, conducted contact surveys in 2015 in high-burden areas. These surveys covered household and neighbor contacts within a 300-meter radius of cases registered in the past decade. Community health workers identified suspects, who were later confirmed by healthcare workers. This approach consistently increased case detection rates, aiming for earlier detection and reduced transmission among high-risk groups. Egypt achieved the WHO leprosy elimination target at the national level in 1994 and at the governorate and district levels by 2004. However, 18 villages in six governorates, primarily in the southern region, have yet to meet this goal. Approximately 60% of new leprosy cases in Egypt originate from these areas. The Ministry of Health and Population has intensified efforts in these hotspots, focusing on early detection, active screening, community awareness, stigma reduction, and rehabilitation of patients. In Paraguay, the Mennonite Hospital Km 81 serves as a referral center for leprosy treatment and training for healthcare professionals. Nursing students are required to participate in practical lessons at this hospital and conduct health education and active screening in their communities. This initiative, started in 2009, has increased case detection and awareness at minimal financial cost. MDT, a combination of drugs, is the cornerstone of leprosy treatment, preventing drug resistance. MDT is provided free of charge globally through WHO coordination, with distribution managed by national health ministries. Ensuring no shortages of MDT at health facilities is critical to starting treatment promptly and preventing disease transmission. MDT is safe during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and for HIV-positive patients. Treatment duration is six months for PB cases and 12 months for multibacillary (MB) cases. In cases of severe drug intolerance or resistance, alternative treatment regimens are available at specialized centers. MDT is highly effective, with relapse rates being rare when treatment is completed properly. Relapse cases are generally treated with the same MDT regimen. Side effects of MDT are rare but can include minor issues like red urine or gastrointestinal upset, which can be managed with reassurance or food intake. Severe side effects, such as allergic reactions or jaundice, require stopping the drug and referral to specialized care. Leprosy programs aim for a treatment completion rate above 95%. Strategies include patient-centered care, direct observation of treatment (DOT) for high-risk cases, and operational research on treatment adherence. Preventing disabilities involves early diagnosis, timely treatment of reactions, and education on self-care for patients with sensory impairments. Patients with Grade 1 Disability (G1D) or G2D require lifelong care to prevent further complications. Leprosy reactions, such as reversal reactions (Type 1) and erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL, Type 2), are the main causes of disability. These reactions can occur before, during, or after MDT treatment, necessitating post-treatment care and monitoring. Severe reactions require referral and treatment with steroids or high-dose clofazimine. Early treatment of reactions is crucial to prevent disabilities. Patients with recent nerve damage (less than six months) may benefit from steroid treatment, while long-standing damage is often irreversible. Education on recognizing reaction symptoms and the importance of early reporting is vital for all leprosy patients.
